title: Use cases for sealed classes and interfaces

blocks.text: 2.5.3 Use Cases for Sealed Classes and Interfaces

In one week the order service sent shipping emails whose tracking link ended in `/track/null`, and answered a declined card with HTTP 500 because a new endpoint never caught `DeclinedException`, and both bugs compiled. A sealed type can make the compiler, or a constructor, refuse each of them, at a price. How a switch over a sealed type is checked is unit 1.5.4's subject; here we choose where to use one.
A Sealed Result Makes an Expected Failure a Value the Caller Has to Match
A declined card is not a bug: the gateway declines cards every day. `charge` can throw, or it can return one of two records:
We charge four cards in a stream, once through `chargeOrThrow`, which throws `DeclinedException`, and once through `charge`, which returns a `Result`. The gateway declines cards ending in 0:

throwing: batch ended with card 4120 declined
result:   charged 4111
result:   not charged: card 4120 declined
result:   charged 4133
result:   not charged: card 4140 declined

The exception ended the batch at the second card. Card 4111 had been charged, and its receipt was lost with the list. The `Result` version kept going and reported every card. A checked exception would not help in a stream, since it can't leave the lambda (unit 3.2.2).
`describe` switches over the result without a `default`. One that names only `Success` fails to build:

Forgot.java:7: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values
        return switch (r) {
               ^
1 error

The switch is the only check. A caller that drops the value, `charge("4120");`, compiles without a warning, even under `-Xlint:all`, and so does an `instanceof` with no `else`. Each layer passes a failure on by hand, and there is no stack trace (here `charge` takes only the card):

Use a `Result` for outcomes the caller acts on, a decline or a validation error. A bug, a null argument or a broken invariant, still throws: nobody can act on it but the developer, who needs the trace (unit 3.2.4).
<!-- practice 1 -->
Give Each State Its Own Record, and an Order Without a Tracking Number Can't Be Shipped
The order kept a status enum and one nullable field per state:
The warehouse sets `SHIPPED` when the parcel leaves; the carrier sends the tracking number an hour later. The email's switch over `status` names all three constants. It ran in that hour:
Track it: https://carrier.example.com/track/null
Nothing ties `trackingNo` to `SHIPPED`. With a sealed interface, each state is a record that holds exactly the data true in that state, and each transition takes the state it starts from:
static Shipped ship(Paid p, String trackingNo) { return new Shipped(p.paymentId(), trackingNo); }
Shipping a pending order no longer compiles, and shipping without a number fails where it happens, not in a customer's inbox:
ship(paid, null): java.lang.NullPointerException: trackingNo

The record alone doesn't refuse the null: without the compact constructor, `new Shipped("pay-7781", null)` builds and prints `trackingNo=null`. The hour between leaving the warehouse and getting a number becomes a fourth permitted state, `Dispatched(paymentId)`, with no tracking number for the email to print. The cost: every transition builds a new object, and whatever stores or serializes an order must record which record it holds.
<!-- practice 2 -->
An Enum Is Still the Right Choice When a Variant Carries No Data

When every variant is one fixed value, an enum gives more: `values()`, `valueOf` for a database column, `EnumSet` and `EnumMap`, and one instance per value. A sealed interface has none of these. Its variants are classes, and `getPermittedSubclasses()` lists classes, not values (unit 2.5.1).
The trouble starts when one variant needs data per order. A constant is one shared instance, so a field on it belongs to every order at once:
first order's tracking number: CX-20932
The second order overwrote the first one's number. A sealed interface can mix both designs, since an enum may be one of its permitted subtypes (unit 2.5.2).
A Sealed Exception Hierarchy Lets One catch Answer Every Failure, and a New One Breaks the Build

The payment endpoint must turn every gateway failure into an HTTP answer. An exception must extend `Throwable`, so the base is a sealed class, not an interface of records. It is abstract, so the switch needs no case for the base itself (unit 2.5.2):
The usual alternative is a catch clause per subtype:

Both versions answer cards 4111, 4105, 4151 and 4199 the same way. javac doesn't count the clauses as covering the sealed base: without `throws PaymentException`, the clause version fails with `unreported exception PaymentException; must be caught or declared to be thrown`. Now the gateway adds `FraudHold` to the `permits` list, and javac reports only the switch:

Gateway.java:35: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values
            return switch (e) {
                   ^
1 error
With a case added there, card 4166 shows what the clause version does:
4166: 403 held for fraud review | escaped: FraudHold: held for fraud review
The fraud hold left the endpoint as an unhandled exception, a 500. Seal a family of exceptions when one handler must answer all of them; leave it open when callers only catch the base.
Public Sealed Interfaces Over Package-Private Records Let Callers Match but Not Implement

A shipping library returns tracking states. Callers must switch over them, and must not build a `Delivered` the carrier never reported. Public records fail the second rule: anyone can call their constructor. Package-private records fail the first: a caller can't name them in a case:
The library publishes one sealed interface per variant, each permitting a hidden record:
A caller in another package switches over `Tracking.InTransit` and `Tracking.Delivered` with no `default`:

P-31 is at Leipzig
D-07 was signed for by Jane Doe
If it implements `Delivered` itself, javac refuses:
app/Fake.java:6: error: class is not allowed to extend sealed class: Delivered (as it is not listed in its 'permits' clause)

The cost is two types per variant, and callers lose record patterns, since an interface has no components. Their tests can't build a `Delivered` either, so the library ships a factory for them. A public final class with a package-private constructor gives the same guarantees with one type: `new` from another package fails with `is not public in Delivered`.
<!-- practice 4 -->
An Expression Tree Is Records and a Recursive switch: Keep the Walk Exhaustive, Only the Rules Partial

A pricing rule, a search query or a formula is a tree. Each node is a record, and each operation is a function with one switch, no visitor needed: this program's `eval` and `show` are one switch each. Nested record patterns (unit 1.5.3) let a rewrite rule match a shape two levels deep in one case:

expression:  (1 * (x + 2 * 3) + 0 * x)
at x = 4:    10
simplified:  (x + 6)
Rules never cover every tree, so the rule switch needs its `default`. Written as one switch, the rules and the recursion share it:
We added `record Neg(Expr operand)` to `permits`. javac reported `eval`, `show` and the walk, and not `simplifyOneSwitch`. With cases added to the three it named, simplifying `Neg(2 * 3)`:

simplify:          -(6)
simplifyOneSwitch: -(2 * 3)
The one-switch version never looks inside the new node. The price of the split is that every operation lists every node, which suits a tree whose operations grow faster than its node types.
<!-- practice 3 -->
Summary

items: **A sealed `Result` makes an expected failure a value.** A batch keeps going and a switch must name `Failure`, but a dropped result compiles and each layer passes failures on by hand.
**A record per state holds only that state's data.** A transition that takes `Paid` refuses a `Pending` at compile time; the compact constructor, not the record, refuses a null.
**An enum stays right for fixed variants without data**; a field on a constant is shared by everyone.

**A sealed exception base lets one catch switch over every failure**, and a new subtype breaks that switch. javac doesn't count one clause per subtype as covering the base, so the method declares the base and a new subtype escapes.
**Public sealed interfaces over package-private records** let callers match but not implement or construct; their tests need a factory.
**An expression tree is records plus a recursive switch.** Keep the walk free of `default`, so a new node breaks the build.

blocks.text: Reference
**Which design refuses which mistake (javac 21):**

rows: record per state, transitions typed by state
`new Shipped(id, null)` unless the compact constructor checks
a new subtype the switch doesn't name
catch clauses that miss it, when the method declares the base
implementing a variant; naming or building a record
a new node the walk doesn't handle

blocks.text: **Enum or sealed interface:**

rows: no: one shared instance per constant

blocks.text: Challenges

items: Your service has 40 methods that throw `OrderNotFoundException`. Which would you move to a `Result`, and what does each caller have to change?
The order states gain `Cancelled`, reachable from `Pending` and `Paid` but not from `Shipped`. Write the transition methods so a wrong one doesn't compile, and count what else changes.
The shipping library must add `Lost`, and some callers can't recompile this quarter. How would you ship it, and what do those callers' switches do meanwhile?

blocks.text: Design Note: A Public Sealed Type Makes Every New Variant a Breaking Change

Inside one codebase, the compile error a new variant causes is the point: it lists every switch to update. Across a library boundary the same error lands in code the library team doesn't own, and callers who don't recompile get a `MatchException` when the new variant reaches their switch (unit 1.5.4). A library that seals a public type promises its variants as part of its API, so it adds one only in a release that may break callers. When the set must grow freely, a `non-sealed` branch (unit 2.5.2) or a plain interface lets it grow without breaking callers.
